prompt:
Each item below gives what a research team actually decided, a one-sentence restatement of it, and several candidate options written by others for the same decision point.

For each item answer:
- "faithful": "yes" if the restatement describes the same decision as what the team decided (abstracting away study-specific details is fine), "no" if it changes, drops the core of, or adds to the decision.
- "same": for each candidate label, "same" if the candidate is essentially the team's decision (a reader who knew what the team did would say the team took this option, or it contains the team's decision as a part), else "different".

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "faithful": "yes" | "no", "same": {"<label>": "same" | "different"}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key d6e15e422e88
What the team decided: Argues that the real worry is losing control of capabilities, goals and plans rather than capabilities per se, so understanding them in detail is worthwhile.
Restatement: Treat the real concern as losing control of model capabilities, goals and plans rather than capabilities as such, and keep studying them in detail instead of avoiding publication.
C1: Treat understanding research as carrying modest capabilities risk, and review each result for architecture or training insights before deciding whether to publish it in full.
C2: Publish understanding-focused findings openly and do not treat their small incidental capabilities relevance as a reason to withhold or delay any single result.

=== key ae42c37b4625
What the team decided: Points out that capabilities can improve without any understanding, so capability progress should not be attributed to understanding-focused work.
Restatement: Note that capabilities can improve without any understanding of why, such as through architecture sweeps, and do not attribute capability progress to understanding-focused work.
C1: Compare past capability gains against their sources, tracing each to interpretability, optimization, or RLHF-style work, before judging whether understanding work drives progress.
C2: Judge by visible track record: treat interpretability and understanding work as not driving capability gains, and publish findings such as reversal failures without extra review.

=== key 18b7b1dc166d
What the team decided: Notes academics' skepticism that these concepts are overhyped, and expects it to shift as models become more agentic, while still treating them as worth measuring.
Restatement: Acknowledge that academics see these concepts as overhyped, expect that to shift as models grow more agentic, and still treat situational awareness as worth measuring.
C1: Treat situational awareness as measurable only through narrow operational definitions, and add controls and caveats to published results that address academic skepticism directly.
C2: Conclude that situational awareness and self-knowledge are meaningful to measure, and continue the work with evaluation groups rather than engaging the academic skeptics.

=== key 95c4f9ede2b9
What the team decided: He declines to give a point estimate and argues that even a small probability of near-term AI justifies taking it seriously.
Restatement: Decline to give a specific point estimate of AGI arrival and say that even a small chance of near-term AGI is a huge deal that deserves to be taken very seriously.
C1: State a deliberately wide probability distribution over AGI arrival dates, label it a low-confidence personal view, and decline to give a single specific median year.
C2: Give a specific median year for AGI and a rough ninety percent interval, and state it plainly as a personal best guess rather than burying it in qualifications.

=== key 1934d3bdc65f
What the team decided: He recommends investing in alignment research as a bet even when the probability of near-term AGI is fairly low.
Restatement: Invest in more alignment research today as a good bet, even if the probability that AGI arrives soon is fairly low and the kind of system to align is still unclear.
C1: Split effort across scenarios, funding alignment work that stays useful whether AGI is near or far, such as interpretability, evaluations and robustness research.
C2: Prioritize alignment work on current scaled language models, assuming AGI is near, and put most effort into empirical experiments on today's deployed systems.

=== key de1712952274
What the team decided: He recommends building systematic tests of generalization, such as Chollet's benchmark of Raven's-matrices-style tasks, including language-focused versions.
Restatement: Build systematic tests of generalization, such as a benchmark of Raven's-matrices-style reasoning puzzles that includes language-focused versions, beyond standard NLP benchmarks.
C1: Build held-out tasks verified absent from training data, vary their surface form and difficulty, and compare model results against human baselines and memorization controls.
C2: Probe the model with a broad set of new, creative tasks of the kind already tried, and treat consistent success across them as sufficient evidence of real generalization.

=== key 081358a1cb6b
What the team decided: He suggests watching economic uptake through the GPT-3 API as a measure of real-world robustness.
Restatement: Watch economic uptake, meaning how many companies adopt the model through its public API, as a measure of whether it is flexible and robust enough for real-world use.
C1: Test the model under distribution shift, adversarial prompts, paraphrases and long-horizon realistic tasks, and report failure rates with confidence intervals for each condition.
C2: Run the model on a small pilot study of realistic user tasks and treat acceptable performance there as enough to call it flexible and robust for real-world use.

=== key f72c8994ac0c
What the team decided: He argues that forecasts about architectural limits, such as needing richer models than transformers, have a poor track record.
Restatement: Treat forecasts of the capabilities a given architecture can reach, such as claims that richer models than the current standard are needed, as having a poor track record.
C1: Treat capability prediction from architecture and scale as unreliable beyond aggregate loss, and plan for surprise by running broad capability evaluations at every scale step.
C2: Rely on scaling trends to forecast capabilities for a given architecture and scale, and plan around those extrapolations without extra capability evaluations.

=== key 16ec0d86cb46
What the team decided: He points to small-scale experiments or theory as the available methods, while noting uncertainty about how well they transfer to the real problem.
Restatement: Use small-scale experiments on current systems or work on theory, while accepting that it is uncertain how well either transfers to the real alignment problem.
C1: Study alignment problems on today's weaker models with controlled experiments, and label each result by how far it plausibly extends to future more powerful systems.
C2: Skip waiting for powerful systems and run ambitious experiments on current large language models, treating the results as direct evidence about future alignment difficulty.

=== key 8b26e2338757
What the team decided: He argues that alignment must also stay competitive with systems trained other ways, which pure imitation cannot do.
Restatement: Require that aligned systems stay competitive with systems trained in other ways that may be unaligned, and judge imitation by whether it can match them on an even playing field.
C1: Test imitation by measuring whether a human-imitating model matches human behavior on hard tasks, and check whether training it to imitate already requires solving alignment.
C2: Adopt imitation of humans as the working alignment strategy and investigate how far imitators can be amplified beyond human level, without first resolving the presupposition.

=== key 0a47629651f3
What the team decided: Focused on clear falsehoods where the model could have done better, and did not count cases where it retracts or corrects itself.
Restatement: Count only clear falsehoods where the model could plainly have done better as failures, and do not count cases where the model retracts or corrects itself.
C1: Count any false statement as a failure, score informativeness on a separate axis, and report both scores together for every model rather than a single combined number.
C2: Treat truthfulness as calibration, score a statement as a failure only when the model asserts something false with confidence, and give vague non-answers no penalty.

=== key 306e09dd715e
What the team decided: Recommends testing rigorously across a wide range of question types, including very specific facts, and showing the model reliably avoids hallucination and falsehood.
Restatement: Test the model rigorously across a wide range of question types, including very specific facts, and show that it reliably avoids hallucination and falsehood, even in hard-to-evaluate areas.
C1: Combine informal reading of many answers with a quantitative truthfulness benchmark across many domains, and add expert verification on a sample of the hardest technical answers.
C2: Run one quantitative truthfulness benchmark across many domains and report its headline score as the measure of how reliably truthful the model is, skipping manual reading.
